enrichment.short_title: Ship mortgagee's Panama arrest not a breach of equitable duties or trading-contract obligation
key_facts: Den Norske Bank lent US$6 million secured on three Cyprus-registered vessels and a guarantee governed by English law after repeated events of default.

The Bank arrested Tropical Reefer in Panama while laden with bananas; cargo disposal costs and a cargo claim reduced sale proceeds, and the Bank then pursued Acemex under the guarantee for about US$815,000.
Guarantors argued the Bank should have waited to arrest in Germany and that arrest interfered with the shipowner's contracts of carriage.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from summary judgment in the Commercial Court on a guarantee claim following vessel arrest and sale.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; summary judgment for the Bank upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A mortgagee exercising contractual powers of arrest and sale after default is not bound to defer enforcement to maximise sale proceeds or to avoid cargo-related costs, and general equitable duties on sale require reasonable care to obtain a proper price at the date of sale rather than a duty to choose the most advantageous time or place; ship-mortgage authorities on non-interference with charterers' contracts do not assist guarantors where the loan and mortgage documents expressly authorise arrest and sale on default.
legal_issues: Whether a mortgagee owed equitable duties when arresting and selling a laden ship in Panama rather than in Germany
Whether arrest breached an implied obligation not to interfere with the mortgagor's contracts of employment of the vessel
Whether any such breach discharged or reduced the guarantors' liability

enrichment.short_title: Landfill planning permission quashed for failure to assess best practicable environmental option

statutes_considered.name: Town and Country Planning (Environmental Impact Assessment) (England and Wales) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Derbyshire County Council granted planning permission in December 2002 for landfill of about 850,000 cubic metres of waste at Smith's void, former Glapwell Colliery, to reclaim a despoiled site.

Local resident Mr Blewett, who complained of dust, odour and noise from existing nearby landfills, challenged the decision by judicial review on environmental-statement, waste-objective and BPEO grounds.
The council's officer reports addressed noise and odour mitigation but did not carry out a proper BPEO analysis in line with Waste Strategy 2000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of grant of planning permission after permission granted on 29 April 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded on ground (3) only; planning permission quashed; permission to appeal granted on BPEO point of principle; council ordered to pay 50% of claimant's costs.
enrichment.ratio: A waste planning authority must treat BPEO policies in Waste Strategy 2000 as requiring development to be in line with BPEO assessment rather than as a discretionary material consideration, and failure to undertake a proper BPEO analysis can make landfill permission unlawful even where environmental-statement and waste-framework objective challenges fail; deficiencies in an environmental statement do not automatically deprive the authority of power to grant permission where the document reasonably meets Schedule 4 requirements.
legal_issues: Whether the environmental statement unlawfully deferred groundwater and human-health assessment and mitigation
Whether the council failed to keep waste-framework objectives on noise and odour in mind
Whether permission was granted without the required BPEO assessment under Waste Strategy 2000

enrichment.short_title: Permission refused to appeal fragmented UCL employment tribunal decisions
key_facts: Miss Riniker, a German teacher at University College London for about 15 years, brought multiple separate tribunal claims from 1992 onwards alleging unfair dismissal, equal pay/pension discrimination and sex discrimination.

enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused on all four applications.
enrichment.ratio: The Court of Appeal on permission applications reviews only errors of law in the employment tribunal, not EAT procedure; fragmented tribunal claims must be treated as separate proceedings; section 32 Limitation Act 1980 does not apply to equal pay time limits; equal pay and sex discrimination claims are mutually exclusive; preliminary hearings and case-management splitting are Article 6 compliant; absence from hearings after deliberate non-attendance does not breach fair trial rights.

Whether equal pay claim 8812/94 was in time and distinct from sex discrimination
Whether tribunal case management unlawfully fragmented the claimant's overall case
Whether unfair-dismissal jurisdiction and contract conclusions were legally flawed

enrichment.short_title: Neighbour boundary corrected where judge misaligned fence line with 1980 evidence
key_facts: Neighbours disputed the boundary between 8 and 6 Greystone Gardens over roughly 150mm affecting a planned extension; the county court judge ordered removal of fence posts and awarded £20,625 damages.
Evidence showed a 1980 fence marked the boundary, a 1992 brick planter was wholly south of that fence, and concrete post Datum B aligned with the former fence line.
The judge's credibility findings against the appellants did not justify placing the boundary south of Datum B.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Willesden County Court boundary, injunction and damages judgment, with further rulings on damages and costs after appeal judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on boundary line; mandatory injunction and damages award set aside; appellants awarded 30% of costs below and 60% of appeal costs; £500 recompense for fence removal.
enrichment.ratio: Boundary determination requires analysis of physical features and historical use, not automatic preference for one party's witnesses; where a 1980 fence was accepted as marking the boundary and a 1992 planter sat entirely south of it, the boundary should follow that fence alignment through Datum B; an interim injunction over brick piers was not an effective cause of delay damages where the central dispute was fence position at Datum B.
legal_issues: Where the true boundary lay between Datum A and Datum B
Whether credibility findings against the Kupfers determined the boundary line
Whether an injunction over brick piers caused the respondent's building delay and damages
How costs should reflect success on the central boundary issue

enrichment.short_title: Confiscation order quashed where late-joining conspirator obtained no benefit
key_facts: Olubitan was convicted of conspiracy to defraud involving Silverbrook Ltd's mobile phone and computer equipment frauds in late 2000.
Successful consignments worth about £246,000 were obtained before Olubitan joined the conspiracy on 7 December 2000; his only involvement was a dummy consignment intercepted by police.
The trial judge ordered confiscation of £88,199.53 as half the conspirators' total benefit, but the realisable amount was not appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) against confiscation order by leave of the single judge.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 71(4) of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 a defendant's benefit is the value of property he personally obtained or the pecuniary advantage he derived; joining an existing conspiracy makes a defendant guilty of the offence but does not automatically attribute earlier conspiratorial gains to him for confiscation, and where a late joiner obtained nothing from his own participation a confiscation order cannot be based on speculative sharing of earlier proceeds.
legal_issues: Whether a conspirator who joins late is liable for confiscation based on total conspiracy proceeds
Proper construction of 'benefit' and 'obtains' in section 71(4)
Application of R v McKechnie to defendants with limited participation

enrichment.short_title: English service out set aside for Venezuelan oil-pollution reinsurance disputes
key_facts: London-market reinsurers sought declarations that they need not indemnify Bermudan/Venezuelan PDV Insurance in respect of two PDVSA pipeline pollution losses in Venezuela in 1998 and 2001.
Gross J had permitted service out on grounds including English law, London placing and alleged jurisdiction clauses in reinsurance slips.
Moore-Bick J held the attached dispute clause applied only to US/Canadian claims, not the whole contract, and Venezuela was the appropriate forum.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside orders permitting service of English declaration proceedings out of the jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Orders for service out set aside in both actions; proceedings in England not to continue.
enrichment.ratio: An agreement to submit to English jurisdiction is a strong factor favouring service out, but a disputes clause attached to a London-market slip may apply only to the US/Canadian jurisdiction condition it identifies rather than the whole reinsurance contract; where pollution losses, witnesses, documents and Venezuelan limitation and notification issues are centred in Venezuela, England is not clearly the appropriate forum despite English governing law on the reinsurance contract.
legal_issues: Whether reinsurance slips contained an effective English jurisdiction clause for all disputes
Whether England was clearly the appropriate forum under Spiliada
Whether limitation, notification, causation and landowner-contract issues were better tried in Venezuela

enrichment.short_title: Seven-day rescission period not extended after late discovery of VAT petition winding up
key_facts: Oakwood Storage Services Ltd lost bonded-warehouse approval, was struck off and restored to the register, while Customs pursued a VAT assessment and presented a petition based on an estimated £18,304 liability.
The petition was served at the former registered office the directors no longer accessed; the company was wound up on 9 April 2003 before directors discovered the order in mid-April.
Directors applied to rescind the winding-up order in June 2003, over seven days late, while Customs owed substantial tribunal costs that likely exceeded the petition debt.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to High Court against registrar's refusal to extend time to apply to rescind a winding-up order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; refusal to extend time under rule 7.47(4) upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Rule 7.47(4) requires rescission applications within seven days for good reason; where directors learned of a winding-up order in mid-April but delayed until June without urgency, without adequate explanation and without evidence supporting extension, the registrar properly exercised discretion to refuse extension even though a timely application might have succeeded on the merits given a cross-claim to costs exceeding the petition debt.
legal_issues: Whether the VAT petition was validly served at the registered office
Whether the registrar misdirected herself on service, bond security and proportionality
Whether there was sufficient excuse to extend time under rule 7.47(4)

enrichment.short_title: Sierra Leone allowed late contract claims after abandoning embassy fraud case
key_facts: Sierra Leone assigned its London embassy lease at 33 Portland Place to Capricorn, a Nevis company controlled by Edward Davenport, for £50,000 under a 1999 agreement promising refurbishment and an underlease or alternative embassy accommodation.

After expert inspection in August 2003 showed the 1999 leasehold interest had negative value and no refurbishment had occurred, the government abandoned its £5 million fraud claim on the eve of trial.
It sought extensive amendments to plead uncertainty, section 2 invalidity, breach of contract and alter-ego liability against Davenport.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Pre-trial applications to amend pleadings, strike out alter-ego allegations, discharge a worldwide freezing order and grant property-preservation relief.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to amend granted; alter-ego/agency pleading allowed; freezing order against Davenport discharged; injunction granted restraining Capricorn from dealing with Portland Place.
enrichment.ratio: Late radical amendments may be permitted where a fraud claim is abandoned as groundless, the proposed uncertainty, section 2 and breach claims are seriously arguable, delay is partly attributable to the defendant obstructing inspection, and the defendant cannot show irremediable prejudice; a controlling shareholder may be sued on a company contract if pleaded facts could infer agency or nominee status, but a long-standing freezing order based on abandoned fraud should be discharged where substantial damages are not the primary remedy sought.
legal_issues: Whether late amendments should be allowed after abandonment of the fraud claim
Whether Capricorn could be treated as Davenport's alter ego, agent or nominee
Whether the worldwide freezing order against Davenport should continue
Whether Capricorn should be restrained from disposing of Portland Place

enrichment.short_title: Coroner inquest verdict upheld despite fresh medical evidence on head injury delay
key_facts: John Bunker suffered a head injury during a scuffle with a shop manager in February 2001, declined hospital transport after ambulance assessment, was arrested and later vomited at the police station before hospital treatment; he died the next day.
A jury inquest in November 2001 returned accidental death after Rule 37 statements were read for absent witnesses and an adjournment request was refused.
Post-inquest reports from consultants Gavalas and Watkins suggested earlier treatment might have improved survival chances.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of inquest verdict and application under section 13 Coroners Act 1988 for a fresh inquest.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review claim dismissed; application for fresh inquest refused.
enrichment.ratio: Rule 37 admission of witness statements is lawful where evidence is unlikely to be disputed and no timely objection is made; restriction of cross-examination to conduct rather than policy guidance is proper; alleged delay between police station departure and hospital treatment does not establish a large unexplained gap on the evidence; fresh medical opinion based on fuller treatment assumptions does not make a fresh inquest necessary where the inquest was not a death-in-custody neglect case and any clinical failings are better pursued in civil proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether Rule 37 use of witness statements rendered the inquest unfair
Whether cross-examination was improperly restricted
Whether the coroner should have adjourned for new medical evidence
Whether fresh expert evidence required a fresh inquest under section 13

enrichment.short_title: Consumer credit enforceability point allowed after failure to seek extension of time
key_facts: Mrs Turner borrowed in 1992 secured on her Formby home; possession proceedings began in 1993 and she later sought to counterclaim that the agreement was not properly executed under the Consumer Credit Act 1974.
District Judge Bryce limited the counterclaim in March 2001; permission to appeal was granted eight months late without an extension application or supporting evidence.
Judge Appleton dismissed the appeal for want of extension of time, though he considered the enforceability argument had merit.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal resolving appeal route, then allowing appeal from circuit judge's refusal to extend time to appeal a county court case-management order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; defendant permitted to pursue enforceability declaration as a preliminary issue subject to no restitution of past payments; defendant to pay costs of appeals.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to apply for extension of time to appeal is an irregularity curable under CPR 3.10 and 3.9 where justice requires; a conditional order barring restitution can mitigate prejudice; a borrower should be allowed to try whether a regulated agreement was improperly executed under sections 60-65 and section 127(3) as a preliminary issue rather than leaving enforceability unresolved until possession enforcement.
legal_issues: Correct appeal route from a circuit judge's time-limit decision
Whether CPR 3.10 permitted waiver of missing extension application and evidence
Whether the borrower should be allowed to plead improper execution and section 127(3) unenforceability
Appropriate costs and conditional orders
